name: Battle of Verdun
info: The German 5th Army attacked the French defences at Verdun on the Western Front in 1916 to draw in and wear down the French army; after 302 days the French had recovered most of the ground and the Germans had failed to reach their aim.

facts.date: 21 February to 18 December 1916 (302 days), in four phases
facts.place: The hills on the right (east) bank of the Meuse north of Verdun, later also the west bank, in the Fortified Region of Verdun, north-eastern France
facts.sides: Germany: the 5th Army under Crown Prince Wilhelm, within the plan of Erich von Falkenhayn, with 1,201 guns massed on the front, two thirds heavy or super-heavy. France: the Second Army and the Fortified Region of Verdun, under Philippe Pétain from late February, then Robert Nivelle, with 388 field guns and 244 heavy guns at the start of the attack
facts.outcome: The Germans captured Fort Douaumont and Fort Vaux but never reached the Meuse Heights as a secure position; French counter-offensives in October and December recovered both forts and much of the ground. Casualties are put at about 714,000 in all, by Heer and Naumann and by Philpott.

t: Falkenhayn planned to take the Meuse Heights so that the French would send their reserves to recapture them and suffer heavy losses; historians disagree whether attrition was his aim from the start or was put forward after the attack failed.
The battle lasted 302 days and was the longest of the First World War; Heer and Naumann calculated 377,231 French and 337,000 German casualties, while other historians give different totals.
In France Verdun came to stand for the determination of the army and the destructiveness of the war, and in 1984 Helmut Kohl and François Mitterrand stood together at the Douaumont cemetery.
dyk: Fort Douaumont, the largest fort of the Verdun region, held only a maintenance crew of about 68 technicians in February 1916, and a German party of about 100 soldiers entered it through an unmanned ditch bunker.
ev: Resources are taken from the forts of Verdun, and the railway line from Paris is closed by the German 3rd Army in mid-July
A bombardment by 808 guns opens Operation Judgement on 21 February and German infantry attack in the afternoon
German troops enter Fort Douaumont, held by a small maintenance crew
The Germans extend the offensive to the west bank to destroy the French artillery
Fort Vaux surrenders on 7 June, and the German advance of 23 June reaches Chapelle Sainte-Fine, its furthest point
Falkenhayn orders the Germans onto the defensive after the failed attack on Fort Souville
French marines and colonial infantry recapture Fort Douaumont
A French offensive under Mangin takes 11,387 prisoners and recovers the ground lost in February

sections.background:
After the German advance in France was halted at the First Battle of the Marne in 1914, offensives on the Western Front in 1914 and 1915 gained little ground and cost many casualties. According to his memoirs, the Chief of the German General Staff, Erich von Falkenhayn, believed that victory might no longer come from a decisive battle but that the French army could be defeated if it suffered enough casualties. He offered five corps from the strategic reserve for an attack at Verdun, on the east bank of the Meuse only.

The plan rested on German heavy artillery, which had been used against Russian defences in the Gorlice–Tarnów Offensive of 1915 and had inflicted what are described as extraordinary casualties on the French in the Second Battle of Champagne. By taking or threatening Verdun, the Germans expected the French to send in their reserves to attack secure German positions, and the British to launch a relief offensive that would also fail. If France then refused to negotiate, a second phase would attack the weakened armies.

The Fortified Region of Verdun lay in a salient formed in 1914. It had a double ring of 28 forts and smaller works. General Joseph Joffre had concluded from the fall of the Belgian fortresses in 1914 that forts were obsolete, and in 1915 the region lost 54 artillery batteries. By 1916 the 18 large forts and other batteries had fewer than 300 guns, and their garrisons were small maintenance crews.
sections.forces:
The German 5th Army, under Crown Prince Wilhelm, divided the front into four areas and received the III Corps, VII Reserve Corps and XVIII Corps, each reinforced by 2,400 experienced troops and 2,000 trained recruits. Ten new rail lines were built, and shelters 4.5 to 14 metres deep were dug for up to 1,200 infantry each. A total of 1,201 guns were massed, two thirds of them heavy or super-heavy, taken from the rest of the Western Front, with ammunition for 2,000,000 rounds in the first six days.

The plan called for limited objectives: the Meuse Heights on a line from Froide Terre to Fort Souville and Fort Tavannes. Artillery was to carry the burden and infantry casualties were to be kept low. The phrase relentless pressure, added by the 5th Army staff, left the purpose of the offensive unclear. Falkenhayn wanted ground from which artillery could dominate the field, while the 5th Army wanted a quick capture of Verdun.

On the French side General Frédéric-Georges Herr held the front with 8 and a half divisions in line and 2 and a half in close reserve. Joffre expected a diversion and had 25 divisions in the strategic reserve. French artillery reinforcements brought the total at Verdun to 388 field guns and 244 heavy guns. Joffre had been warned in January by accurate intelligence of German intentions but considered that an attack would be a diversion.
sections.course:
Bad weather delayed the attack from 12 to 21 February, when a ten-hour bombardment by 808 guns began at 7:15 a.m. Infantry attacked at 4:00 p.m. with flamethrowers, followed by stormtroopers using hand grenades, and the Germans suffered only about 600 casualties. By 22 February they had advanced 5 kilometres, and Colonel Émile Driant was killed at Bois des Caures. On 25 February a German party of about 100 soldiers entered Fort Douaumont through an unmanned ditch bunker and took Warrant Officer Chenot and about 25 men prisoner. Pétain took command that night.

The advance slowed on 27 February, after a thaw and the arrival of French reinforcements. In March the Germans extended the attack to the west bank, towards Mort-Homme and Côte 304, to destroy the French guns there. The attacks cost many casualties, and by the end of March the offensive had cost the Germans 81,607. Falkenhayn began to think of ending the offensive, but the 5th Army staff wanted to go on, and by the end of April he had agreed to wide-front attacks.

The French retook part of Fort Douaumont on 22 May but were cut off and surrendered, 1,000 prisoners being taken. Fort Vaux was taken after a final assault on 1 June, and its 574 survivors surrendered on 7 June. On 23 June the Germans, after a gas bombardment, advanced to Chapelle Sainte-Fine, within about 5 kilometres of the citadel. An attack on Fort Souville failed on 11 and 12 July. In October and December French counter-offensives recovered Douaumont, Vaux and most of the lost ground.
sections.aftermath:
The French recaptured Fort Douaumont on 24 October, after a six-day bombardment of 855,264 shells, and took more than 6,000 prisoners and fifteen guns by 25 October. The Germans evacuated Fort Vaux on 2 November, and the French reached the front line of 24 February on 5 November. The second offensive began on 15 December after a bombardment of 1,169,000 shells. Of 21,000 men in the five German front divisions, 13,500 were lost, most of them taken prisoner. The French took 11,387 prisoners and 115 guns and pushed the closest German point 7.5 kilometres back.

Falkenhayn was replaced on 29 August by Paul von Hindenburg and Erich Ludendorff, who ended the German offensive on 2 September. The general of the 5th Army and a corps commander were sacked on 16 December. The offensives on the Somme and by Brusilov had already forced the Germans to move troops and guns from Verdun, and the Germans were limited to small local attacks after 12 July.

Historians give many casualty totals. Heer and Naumann calculated 377,231 French and 337,000 German, 714,231 in all. Clayton gave 351,000 French, of whom 56,000 were killed, 100,000 missing or prisoners and 195,000 wounded, and 330,000 German, of whom 143,000 were killed or missing. Philpott recorded 377,000 French, 162,000 of them killed, and 337,000 German. The battlefield contains the remains of over 100,000 missing soldiers.
sections.sources:
Casualty figures for Verdun are hard to fix because the records were kept in different ways. Paul Jankowski described how French units produced numerical loss states every five days, while the German armies compiled Verlustlisten every ten days, and medical data was published separately. These records counted losses over time, not by place. Some French data excluded the lightly wounded and some did not, and the German Verlustlisten excluded them. Churchill added 2 per cent to the German figures for unrecorded wounded, and the British official historian James Edmonds added 30 per cent.

Winston Churchill in 1927 gave 442,000 French casualties; Robert Doughty wrote that he and those who followed him had mistakenly included all French losses on the Western Front. In the second edition of The World Crisis in 1938, Churchill gave 278,000 German casualties and deducted an eighth from his figures for other sectors. Terraine, Dupuy and Dupuy, Mason, Grant, Foley and Afflerbach each give figures that differ from these.

The aims of Falkenhayn are also disputed. His memoirs quote a memorandum of December 1915 saying that the forces of France would bleed to death. Holger Afflerbach concluded in 1994 that it was written after the war but reflected his thinking at the end of 1915, while Gerd Krumeich wrote that it was fabricated to justify a failed strategy. Robert Foley wrote in 2007 that Falkenhayn intended a battle of attrition from the beginning, as against the views of Wolfgang Foerster and Krumeich, noting that the loss of documents led to many interpretations.
sections.legacy:
In France the battle came to symbolise the determination of the French army and the destructiveness of the war. It became for the French the representative memory of the First World War, as the Somme is for the United Kingdom. Antoine Prost wrote that like Auschwitz, Verdun marks a transgression of the limits of the human condition. Between 1918 and 1939 the French held two memories of it: a patriotic one in the memorials on the battlefield and in Nivelle's words, They shall not pass, and the survivors' memory of death and suffering.

In 1920 a ceremony in the citadel of Verdun chose the body for the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Arc de Triomphe. Six villages were not rebuilt and became uninhabited communes. Forests planted in the 1930s hide most of the Zone rouge, but the battlefield remains a vast graveyard. Mortal remains found by the French Forestry Service are laid in the Douaumont ossuary.

German commanders of the 5th Army tried to capture Verdun and attacked regardless of loss, and the offensive lasted far longer and took far more infantry than Falkenhayn had intended. French morale suffered: five infantry regiments saw collective indiscipline in 1916, and Lieutenants Henri Herduin and Pierre Millant were shot on 11 June and exonerated after an inquiry in 1926. In the 1960s Verdun became a symbol of Franco-German reconciliation, and in the 1980s a capital of peace. On 22 September 1984 Helmut Kohl and François Mitterrand stood together at the Douaumont cemetery.

summary: The Battle of Verdun lasted from 21 February to 18 December 1916 and was the longest battle of the First World War. The German attack on the Meuse Heights did not gain the position it aimed for, and French counter-offensives recovered most of the ground. Casualties are put at about 714,000.
references: Alistair Horne, The Price of Glory: Verdun 1916 (Penguin, 1981)
P. Jankowski, Verdun: The Longest Battle of the Great War (Oxford University Press, 2014)
R. T. Foley, German Strategy and the Path to Verdun: Erich von Falkenhayn and the Development of Attrition, 1870–1916 (Cambridge University Press, 2007)
I. Ousby, The Road to Verdun: France, Nationalism and the First World War (Jonathan Cape, 2002)
R. A. Doughty, Pyrrhic victory: French Strategy and Operations in the Great War (The Belknap Press of Harvard University, 2005)
notes: The article says Pétain was promoted to command GAC in early May and also, under Morale, that Pétain left the Second Army on 1 June; the text gives only the early May promotion with Nivelle taking over.
Falkenhayn's memorandum in the article reads 'The string in France has reached breaking point', a plain slip for strength; I quote only that the forces of France would bleed to death.

The article gives the German plan's bombardment as 12 February and the delay to 21 February; the end date 18 December is the lead's, while the phase headings run to 17 December and the text says 15-17 December.
German 5th Army casualty figures conflict (Afflerbach 336,000 to 31 August, Foley 281,000 to 31 August, Wendt 336,831 to 20 December); I left these out of the text except as noted.
Left out: the details of the fort construction, Mangin's quip, the Marne-Argonne subsequent operations of 1917 and 1918, the 1917 French attack, Doughty's percentages.

The article says Churchill used 442,000 in 1927 (for Doughty) and also gives the 1938 figures of 442,000 other ranks and 460,000 with officers; I report only the Doughty note and the 1938 German figure.
Spelling Gorlice–Tarnów corrected from a slip.
